paragraphs: Aspen Education Group, based in Cerritos, California, was one of the largest owners of troubled-teen programs in the United States. It ran wilderness programs, therapeutic boarding schools, residential treatment centers and the Wellspring weight-loss camps.{wiki,vb} Backed by private equity, it grew from six programs in 1998 to 31 in 2005.{yt} In 2006 CRC Health Group, owned by Bain Capital, bought it for nearly $300 million.{salon} Children died in its programs throughout its history. Matthew Meyer, 14, died at Lone Star Expeditions in Texas in 2004; Brendan Blum, 14, at Youth Care of Utah in 2007; and Sergey Blashchishen, 16, at SageWalk in Oregon in 2009.{salon} From 2009 to 2014 CRC closed or sold off most of Aspen's programs. Of the 40 programs Kids Over Profits holds records of, in 16 states, Washington, D.C., and England, only Talisman Camps in North Carolina is still open.

Aspen began in December 1997 as Aspen Youth Services, a spin-off of College Health Enterprises, which had itself come out of the CEDU family of schools. It took the name Aspen Education Group in 2001.{rtt,wiki} In 1998 the Sprout Group and Frazier Healthcare Ventures bought major stakes, when its revenue was about $28 million.{wiki} In 2002 Warburg Pincus invested $15 million, and lenders added $48 million or more.{wiki} Bain Capital bought CRC Health, the country's largest for-profit addiction treatment chain, in February 2006, paying $720 million.{vb,salon} CRC announced its purchase of Aspen that October, and Aspen became CRC's youth division.{vb,wiki} In 2014 Acadia Healthcare agreed to buy CRC in a stock deal valued at about $1.175 billion.{tm14}

Accounts of deaths and abuse span the company's history. A post on the survivor forum Fornits says that 17-year-old Brandon Hoffman died by suicide at Mount Bachelor Academy in Prineville, Oregon, on December 16, 1998.{fornits} Matthew Meyer died of heat stroke in 2004, eight days into his stay at Lone Star Expeditions; his family's wrongful-death suit was settled.{salon} In 2007 Brendan Blum, who had Asperger's, died at Youth Care of Utah after staff dismissed his complaints of illness. He had a twisted bowel that needed emergency surgery. A Utah court dismissed criminal negligence charges against two monitors in 2008, and his mother settled a wrongful-death suit.{salon} In 2008 a 16-year-old at Adirondack Leadership Expeditions in New York suffered frostbite severe enough to need eight months of treatment.{salon} On August 28, 2009, Sergey Blashchishen died of apparent heat stroke on his first hike at SageWalk. A Lake County sheriff's deputy wrote that staff actions could amount to criminal mistreatment, and that SageWalk "may have taken children to the precipice of disaster and been lucky."{kgw}

Also in 2009, a seven-month Oregon investigation found nine cases of abuse or neglect involving five students at Mount Bachelor Academy since 2007. Most involved a mandatory program called Lifesteps, in which at least two students were made to act out sexual scenarios in front of staff and peers.{wl} The state gave the school 90 days to fix the problems or lose its license, and it closed that year. CRC said the allegations were false.{wl,wiki,salon} Former students filed three suits over Mount Bachelor: 17 sought $26 million in 2011, then 14 sought $23 million and 13 sought $19.5 million in November 2011 and January 2013.{wiki}

Closures followed in waves. Six Aspen programs closed around 2009.{wiki} On March 24, 2011, Aspen announced that it would close five more and consolidate three, blaming "reduced demand for therapeutic schools and programs in today's economy." The five were Bromley Brook School, New Leaf Academy of Oregon, NorthStar Center, Aspen Ranch and SunHawk Adolescent Recovery Center.{st11} On July 10, 2013, it announced five more: the Academy at Swift River, Talisman Academy, Stone Mountain School, SUWS Adolescent & Youth Programs in Idaho, and Adirondack Leadership Expeditions.{st13} CRC's chief executive, Andrew Eckert, told employees that "gone are the days of student loans for these programs."{ade} That August the Oakley School in Utah, which Aspen had owned since 2004, began a partnership with InnerChange.{wb0913}

Other programs reopened under new owners and new names. Island View Residential Treatment Center became Elevations RTC in 2014, and the Aspen Institute for Behavioral Assessment became ViewPoint Center that May.{wiki} Family Help & Wellness, founded in 2008 by Aspen's former chief financial officer, reopened or rebranded many former Aspen programs.{rtt} Kids Over Profits' records show that Copper Canyon Academy in Arizona became Sedona Sky Academy and Stone Mountain School in North Carolina became Asheville Academy for Girls, and that both closed in 2025.

The sales led to lawsuits. In 2014 Terri and David Myers of Missouri sued Aspen, Island View, CRC Health Group, Bain Capital, the Dr. Phil organization and an Island View teacher, Ryan Mortensen. They said Dr. Phil had recommended Island View for their 15-year-old daughter after a 2013 broadcast, and that her arm was badly broken when Mortensen pulled her off her bed.{chn} Court records show the court dismissed the claims against Bain and the Dr. Phil defendants with prejudice in 2015. Also in 2014, according to court records, the buyers of Island View, Turn-About Ranch, Copper Canyon and the assessment program sued Aspen over payments they said it kept after the sale. Aspen said the buyers had broken the agreement first, and the case was dismissed with prejudice in 2015.
